chapter_theme: Poems 81-100 open with praise of the Chola Porvaikko Perunarkilli, including Nakkannaiyar's three poems of a woman's one-sided love for him, and a mother's boast that her son will be found on the battlefield; the rest is Avvaiyar's run on Athiyaman Neduman Anji: warnings to his foes, the nelli fruit of long life, her poems as a child's prattle, his used and broken spears, his wounds, his threat of tribute and his unabated anger.

81.reading: The poet says Killi's battle cry is louder than the roaring sea and his elephants trumpet without pause like the thunder of the monsoon, and asks who could be more pitiable than those who fall into the hands of this open-handed warrior with his tightly strung aathi garland.
81.nuance: The poem never shows a fight: it measures the king entirely by sound (sea, thunder) and then turns, in a single question, to the victims, so praise is made out of the dread it implies.

thinai_evidence.note: it praises the king's overwhelming strength in war, the matter of arasa vaakai

82.reading: Killi's fight with the champion who came to take his town was over quicker than the needle in the hand of a leather-worker stitching a cot when the festival has begun, his wife is in labour and the rain has come down as the sun sets.
82.nuance: The simile stacks three pressures on one low-status craftsman (the festival trade, the birth, the failing light and rain), so the king's speed is measured by a working man's desperate haste, a rare reach of praise into ordinary life.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem celebrates the king's swift victory over an invader

comparisons.tenor: the speed of the king's battle

83.reading: A woman in love with Killi says she fears her mother if her bangles slip for this young bull of a man with ankleted feet and dark beard, and is ashamed before the assembly to embrace his conquering shoulders; she wishes that this bewildered town, split two ways and never on one side, may tremble with longing as she does.
83.nuance: Her own split (between fear of her mother and shame before others on one side, desire on the other) is set against a town split into two sides; 85 suggests the town is divided as the crowd at a contest, so her curse wishes her inner division onto the spectators. The exact sense of இருபாற் பட்ட is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: a one-sided longing held back by fear and shame, with no answering love

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the woman speaks of herself and wishes her longing on the town; no addressee is named

84.reading: She says her lord has great shoulders though he eats coarse gruel, while she, kept outside his enclosure, has turned the colour of gold; when he goes out to fight, he is to the swaggering warriors of the noisy festive town like a ford the salt-carriers dread.
84.nuance: Two concessions run in parallel (he eats gruel yet is broad-shouldered; I am shut out yet golden), and பொன் here is the gold of பசலை, the pallor of longing, not wealth. Line 1's என்ஜ is a corrupt spelling of என்னை, my lord.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman stays outside and grows pale for a man who does not answer

comparisons.tenor: the king in battle, to the warriors who meet him

85.reading: Because this is not her lord's own town or country, one side of the crowd says he is winning and the other says he is not; she finds both words good, for she ran with her anklets ringing, stood against the palmyra by her house, and saw for herself that he won.
85.nuance: The poem does not say what the contest is; ஆடு is read as victory. A stranger's contest splits the crowd, and the woman, who has no claim on him, settles the dispute only for herself by looking.

thinai_evidence.note: a woman with no tie to him watches his contest from her own house

86.reading: Asked, as she holds the fine post of her small house, where her son is, a mother says she does not know where he is, but the womb that bore him is like a rock den a tiger has left: he will show himself on the battlefield.
86.nuance: The empty den carries the whole boast: the womb is a lair, the son a tiger, and his absence from home is the proof of his nature. The small house (சிற்றில்) sets her poverty against her pride.

thinai_evidence.note: a mother's pride in her son's valour, the household valour of the mullai thurais of vaakai

comparisons.tenor: the mother's womb, and the son who has gone from it

87.reading: Enemies, beware of entering the battlefield: among us is a warrior like the wheel that a carpenter, who makes eight chariots a day, spent a month making.
87.nuance: The vehicle is about care, not size: a craftsman who turns out eight chariots a day gave a whole month to this one wheel, so the warrior is the most thoroughly made thing in the army.

thinai_evidence.note: a warning to the enemy before battle, the boast of an army

88.reading: Whoever you are, mighty ones, do not boast that you will fight us with your rear and van until you have seen my lord, the great chief of the Mazhavar with the gleaming long spear, his broad chest bright with fine ornaments and his drum-like shoulders, a fighter who stands above the festival.

thinai_evidence.note: a warning to foes who boast of fighting

89.reading: To a warlike king who keeps asking whether there are fighters in her broad land, the dancer answers that there are young warriors like snakes that do not fear the striking stick, and besides, her lord, who on hearing the wind strike the taut drum hanging in the common hall says 'that is war!'.
89.nuance: The lord's eagerness is shown by a mistake: he takes the wind on a drum for a call to battle. The dancer's answer turns the king's taunt into a threat.

thinai_evidence.note: a challenge before battle answered with a boast of the army

90.reading: Can deer herds stand where a fierce tiger rages on the slope scented with kaandhal like broken bangles and wild jasmine? Can darkness stay when the sun grows angry? Is there a ford the proud bullock cannot cross as it drags a laden cart over sand and stone? So, lord of the Mazhavar with arms like a gate-bar, are there foes who can stand once you enter the field?
90.nuance: Three rhetorical questions from three orders (beast, sky, labour) all expect 'no', and only the fourth names the king, so the answer is already given before he appears.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's irresistibility in battle

comparisons.tenor: the king entering battle, and the foes as the deer
the king for whom no obstacle is impassable

91.reading: Avvai blesses Anji, lord of the Athiyar, with his true sword, anklet and golden garland, that he may last like the blue-throated one whose head shines with the milk-white crescent, because he gave her the sweet fruit of the small-leaved nelli taken from a hard crag of an ancient mountain, without telling her what it would do, so that she might escape death.
91.nuance: The gift is in what he withheld: by keeping the fruit's virtue to himself (ஆதல் நின்னகத்து அடக்கி) he made sure she would eat it, and so gave up long life for a poet. The blessing matches the gift: life for life, and from the god who survived the poison.

thinai_evidence.note: a blessing on a patron for his gift, which is praise rather than battle

92.reading: A child's prattle does not keep to the lute, does not suit the hour and carries no sense, yet it moves fathers to tenderness; Avvai says her own words are like that, since Neduman Anji, who crossed many guarded walls of his enemies, receives them with grace.
92.nuance: Modesty and praise are one move: by calling her poem prattle she makes the patron a father, so his favour is love, not judgement of merit.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the patron's grace toward her poems

comparisons.tenor: the poet's words to her patron

93.reading: Avvai asks what is left of going to war with drums booming, since the kings who could not even meet the van and ran would have died of sickness and been laid by the four-Veda priests on darbha grass and cut with a sword, so as to go where heroes go; they escaped that rite because they fell on your field, great one, where you crushed the elephants and took a noble wound.
93.nuance: The poem records a rite: a body that died of disease was laid on darbha grass and cut with a sword so that it could go where those who died in battle go. A death without a wound needed a wound. The turn on உய்ந்தனர் (they escaped) is ironic: being killed by Anji saved them from that disgrace. The syntax of lines 2 to 11 is compressed and the reading is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's victory and his noble wound

94.reading: To us you are gentle, great one, like the big bull elephant that lies in the ford while the village boys wash its white tusks; to your enemies you are harsh, like its musth that no one can come near.
94.nuance: One elephant gives both halves: the same animal is a children's plaything and a terror, so the king's two faces are one nature, not a mask.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's excellence, mild to his own and terrible to foes

comparisons.tenor: the king to his own people

95.reading: These spears, decked with peacock feathers and garlands, their thick shafts trimmed and oiled, sit in a guarded mansion; those, their points and edges broken from stabbing enemies, lie in the smith's small shed: they are the sharp spears of our lord, head of the kin of the poor, who gives food when he has it and shares the meal when he has none.
95.nuance: The praise of the other armoury is the insult: spears kept beautiful have never been used. The broken spears and the shared hunger are one portrait: what Anji has is always in use, by his army or his dependants.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the patron's spears and his sharing

96.reading: Two enmities have risen against my young lord with the thumbai on his broad chest and his long, thick arms: one has seized the women who looked at him, whose flower-like eyes grow pale and shoulders thin; the other is the town he goes to, which resents his lodging, asking whether, though there is no festival, his mutton-fed retinue will miss no meal and his elephants will take the water of the ford.
96.nuance: The 'enmities' are a joke of praise: one is the love-sickness he causes, the other the dread of feeding his following, so beauty and power are both counted as trouble he brings. The hosts' complaint in lines 6 to 8 is compressed and its sense is not sure.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a young prince through the effects he has on women and towns

97.reading: Anji's swords lost their shape plunged in flesh as he broke his foes' guarded walls, his spears are loose in their sockets from crushing the toddy-rich lands of fort-holders, his elephants have shed their thick bands battering gates, his horses' hooves are bloodied from trampling warriors' gold garlands, and he himself is like a shield pierced by arrows; so, if you want your old town of rich paddy, pay him tribute, for he will not give way, and if you will not believe it, it will be no wonder if your soft-natured women lose their husbands' shoulders.
97.nuance: Each weapon is praised by its damage, ending with the king as a pierced shield; the threat is made through the enemy's women, whose loss is the last item of the catalogue.

thinai_evidence.note: a warning to enemies built on the army's battle wear, demanding tribute

98.reading: Seeing your elephants with battle-blunted tusks, your foes bar their fort gates; seeing your horses with bloodied hooves, they block the gaps with forked thorns; seeing your sheathed spear, they tighten their grip on their shields; seeing your scarred warriors, they bind up their arrow wounds; you are like the band that stands outside by old custom to carry off the wounded, undeterred even by the smoke of white mustard: so must their wide land, its fields where the bending ears touch the ridges and its great waters, perish while they grieve?
98.nuance: Each sight of Anji's army is answered by a defensive act, and the fourth turns to the wounded; the simile then makes Anji the death that waits outside the sickroom, against which the mustard smoke of the healing rite does nothing. The poem ends in pity for the enemy's rich land, the matter of கொற்றவள்ளை. The identity of the band in lines 15 to 17 is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the closing lament for the enemy country about to be ravaged by the invader

comparisons.tenor: the king, who carries off the wounded foes

99.reading: Like your forebears of the ancient line, who honoured the gods, fed the sacrificial fire, brought here the sugarcane that is hard to obtain and ruled the sea-girt land with the wheel of command, you, with your giving anklets, palmyra garland, flowered groves and freshly bloodied spear, won without fault an undivided inheritance, yet were not content, but fought the seven kings with booming drums; even then you were beyond the singers, and now only Paranar could sing your shoulder that crushed proud Kovalur and bore the fort-breaking wheel.
99.nuance: The poem names another poet: Avvai places her patron beyond ordinary singers and hands the Kovalur victory to Paranar, which shows poets marking a deed as fit for a particular voice. The sense of எழுபொறி நாட்டத்து எழாஅத் தாயம் (line 7) and of பரணன் பாடினன் மற்கொல் (line 12) is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's lineage and his victories

100.reading: Spear in hand, anklets on his feet, sweat on his body and a fresh wound on his throat, wearing in his curly hair the white leaf from the top of a young palmyra with vetchi and vengai flowers, he is like a mighty elephant that has fought a striped tiger; his rage has not yet cooled, those who fought him here did not escape, and the eyes that glared at his enemies stay red even as he looks at his own small son.
100.nuance: The last image tests the anger against the tenderest sight and the anger holds: the poem praises the hero and lets the cost show in the same line.

thinai_evidence.note: the victorious king fresh from battle

links.note: 84 says her lord has great shoulders though he eats புற்கை (coarse gruel); Kural 1065 says that even gruel thin as water (அடுபுற்கை) is sweetest when one's own effort earned it.
links.teaches: The Kural's gruel of the self-reliant poor already stood in the older poem for a strong man's austere fare, cited by a woman as proof of his strength, so the couplet's dignity of plain food draws on a heroic image, not only on poverty.

links.note: 85 describes a crowd split into two sides over the contest, one saying he wins and one saying he does not; 83 curses 'this bewildered town, split two ways and never on one side' (இருபாற் பட்ட).
links.teaches: Read with 85, the divided town of 83 is a crowd taking sides over Killi's contest, so the woman's curse wishes her own inner division onto spectators who argue about the very man she loves.

links.note: Kural 69: a mother who hears her son called worthy rejoices more than when she bore him; in 86 a mother likens her womb to a tiger's empty den and says her son will be found on the battlefield.
links.teaches: The Kural's mother waits to hear others praise her son, while the Purananuru mother does not know where he is and stakes her pride on her womb and the battlefield, which shows that the worth a mother hoped for could be a warrior's death as readily as a good name.

links.note: 86's mother says her son will show himself on the battlefield; in 278 an old mother searches the battlefield and rejoices more than at his birth on finding her son fallen with his body cut apart.
links.teaches: Together the two run from boast to proof: the field where 86's son will 'appear' is the field 278's mother has to search among the corpses, and the joy she measures against the day of birth is the price of the first mother's confidence.

links.note: 87 opens களம்புகல் ஓம்புமின், தெவ்விர் (enemies, beware of entering the field); Kural 771 opens என்னைமுன் நில்லன்மின் தெவ்விர் (enemies, do not stand before my lord).
links.teaches: The Kural's chapter on an army's pride keeps a whole Sangam speech-type, the warning to foes addressed as தெவ்விர் with a prohibitive verb, and swaps Avvai's craftsman's image of strength for the hero-stones of the slain, so the couplet is the genre cut down to its threat.

links.note: Both are Avvai's warnings to Anji's foes under the thurai தானை மறம், each built on the imperative ஓம்புமின் (beware).
links.teaches: Side by side they show the formula's moving part: 87 rests the threat on one unnamed warrior wrought like a month-made wheel, 88 on the chief himself in his finery, so the same prohibition could be backed by the army or by the king.

links.note: 90 asks whether deer herds can stand where a fierce tiger rages; Kural 599 says even a huge, sharp-tusked elephant fears when a tiger attacks.
links.teaches: In both the tiger is the spirit that neither numbers nor size can resist, but Avvai sets it on a herd to praise a king while the Kural sets it on an elephant to teach ookkam, so one image served both royal praise and a general maxim on energy.

links.note: Kural 82: even if it were the medicine of deathlessness, eating it alone while the guest waits outside is not to be wished; in 91 Anji gives Avvai the nelli fruit that keeps death away instead of eating it.
links.teaches: The Kural's extreme case, the food of immortality not eaten alone, has a remembered instance in a chieftain who gave a poet the fruit of long life, so the maxim's hyperbole was also a story the tradition told of a real giver.

links.note: 91 thanks Anji for giving Avvai the nelli fruit so that she might escape death; 235, Avvai's lament for him, recalls how he shared toddy and food with her and says the spear that pierced him fell on the tongues of poets.
links.teaches: The gift of long life in 91 turns bitter in 235: the poet made to outlive her patron is left to mourn him, and the spear that killed the giver silences the singers he fed, so the pair binds the bard's fortune to the patron's life.

links.note: 91 calls Anji lord of the Athiyar with கழல்தொடி தடக்கை; Akananuru 162 names a கழல்தொடி அதிகன் who never fails the hope of suppliants and owns a hill of jackfruit and vengai (probably the same Athiyar house, though the akam poem does not say which chief).
links.teaches: An akam poet uses the same epithet and the same fame for never failing those who ask, which 91 shows in one deed, to set the hill where a lover recalls a hard-won meeting, so the Athiyar chief's giving was a byword love poets could lean on.

links.note: 92: a child's prattle does not keep to the lute and makes no sense, yet moves fathers; Kural 66: those who call the flute and lute sweet have not heard their children's prattle.
links.teaches: The Kural leaves unsaid that prattle fails every test of music, and Avvai says it outright and builds on it, so read together the father's delight is shown to be grace rather than taste, which is what lets her use it for a patron's love of an imperfect poem.

links.note: Kural 776: the hero counts as wasted every day on which he took no noble wound (விழுப்புண்); 93 tells how a king who died of sickness was cut with a sword on darbha grass so as to go where the battle-slain go, and ends on Anji's விழுப்புண்.
links.teaches: The poem shows why a day without a wound could be counted lost: a death without one had to be given a wound by rite before the dead could reach the heroes' world, so the Kural's ledger rests on a belief about where the dead go.

links.note: 94: gentle to us like the bull elephant that lets village boys wash its tusks, harsh to foes like its musth; 315: Anji can stay unseen like the fire-stick tucked in the eaves and blaze like the fire it kindles.
links.teaches: Avvai gives Anji the same two-sided nature twice in different images, gentle and fierce in 94, hidden and blazing in 315, which shows that the double character, not any single image, was her settled portrait of him.

links.note: 95: he gives food when he has it and eats together with the poor when he has none; 315: when he has, he can eat, and he gives to suppliants even beyond what he owes.
links.teaches: Both poems answer the same question, what Anji does when his stores run low, and together show that his fame as a giver rests on sharing want with his dependants, not on abundance.

links.note: Kural 227: the disease called hunger does not touch one used to sharing his food; 95 praises a lord who shares when he has and goes without together with his dependants when he has not.
links.teaches: The Kural promises the habitual sharer freedom from hunger, while Avvai's lord shares and still has empty days, so the poem shows the virtue the Kural rewards at work in a world where sharing did not prevent want but made it common to all.

links.note: 97 lists Anji's swords, spears, elephants and horses worn by war and tells enemies to pay tribute; 98 lists what his enemies do on seeing his elephants, horses, spear and warriors, and ends in pity for their doomed land.
links.teaches: The two catalogues show one army from two sides, its weapons worn out in 97 and the enemy's barred gates and bound wounds in 98, so the tribute demanded in 97 is backed by the ruin of fields that 98 foresees.

links.note: 99 says Anji is beyond ordinary singers and that Paranar sang his victory at Kovalur; in Akananuru 352 the heroine calls her friend's news sweeter than a bard's famous song that set Anji's renown.
links.teaches: The akam heroine's comparison assumes that songs fixing Anji's fame were well known and loved, which 99 confirms by naming a poet who sang it, so a puram repertoire stands behind the love poem's simile.

links.note: 100 ends with the eyes that glared at foes staying red even when he looks at his small son; Kural 775 calls it defeat if the glaring eye blinks when a spear is thrown.
links.teaches: The Kural asks the warrior's glare not to waver before a spear, and Avvai shows it cannot waver even before his own child, so together the fixed red eye is both the warrior's ideal and a cost the poem lets the reader feel.

source_issues: 84 line 1: என்ஜ is a corrupt spelling of என்னை (my lord); read as என்னை.
89 line 2: வாள்நதல் is a misprint for வாள்நுதல் (bright forehead).
93 line 10: நீழ் கழல் is a misprint for நீள் கழல்.
98 line 2: பொர்க் is a misprint for போர்க்.
81 line 3: the semicolon in ஆர்; நார்ச் splits the phrase ஆர் நார் (aathi fibre) that runs into line 4's garland; read without the break.
83's poet is spelled நாய்கண் and 84 and 85's நாய்கன்; one spelling should be chosen.
86: the poet field holds a variant note and a stray heading (காவற் பெண்டு காதற்பெண்டு எனவும் பாடம். பாடப்பட்டோன்) and the patron is None; the poet is காவற் பெண்டு, the rest is not a colophon fact.
99: poet, patron, thinai and thurai are filled from Duraisamy Pillai's edition (show reports FILLED_FROM_DURAISAMY_PILLAI).
98: the colophon gives two thinais (வாகை; வஞ்சியும்) and two thurais (அரச வாகை; கொற்றவள்ளையுமாம்); copied as they stand, both recorded in puram_thurai.

The review's line table lists 83, 86 and 88 as lacking a site line and 95, 99 and 100 as having opening lines the site lacks; our 83, 86 and 88 now have six full lines each and read complete, and the opening lines of 95, 99 and 100 are integral to the syntax (subject, simile or catalogue), so all lines are marked. The review lists 100 among poems with stray glyphs; none remain in the current text.
Patron spelling varies between நெடுமானஞ்சி (87, 88) and நெடுமான் அஞ்சி (89 to 100); spacing only.
